result.instructions: You hold a seat on an agentic council. Use council_wait to wait for your turn, council_submit to act, council_status to look.

tools.name: council_status
tools.description: Where the council stands for your seat: the agenda item, any pending motion, what happened since you last looked, and — if a round is open for you — exactly what you may submit, with reasons. Never blocks.

since.description: show events after this seq (default: since your last look)

tools.name: council_wait
tools.description: Block until a round is open that you have not yet answered, or the meeting adjourns, then return the same view as council_status. Returns early (saying so) after max_wait_s; just call it again. This is how you wait your turn: nobody is penalized for answering slowly.

tools.name: council_submit
tools.description: Submit your sealed intent for the open round. Nobody sees it until the round closes, when everyone's are revealed together. You may replace it until the round closes; only your last counts. `action` must be one of those listed for you in the view.

tools.name: council_record
tools.description: The council's full record so far (minutes): every round, every revealed intent, every outcome. For catching up after arriving late or restarting.

arguments.text: Recommendation for q2: use one independent reviewer from a different model family, not a council of same-substrate members. Reasons: (1) a council drawn from one substrate shares the author's blind spots, so its agreement is coherence, not verification; (2) the 43% vs 116/116 figure is evidence that self-checking by the author misses defects, which supports separating author from checker, but it is about landings, so treat it as a reason to use an independent checker, not as a measured reviewer-type comparison. Conditions: (a) the reviewer is given the plan and the checks to run (dependencies, unstated assumptions, whether each landing check would actually catch a bad result), not only "does this look good"; (b) the reviewer does not see the author's justifications until after writing its own findings, to reduce anchoring; (c) if a council is used, it needs at least one member from a different family, and the record should say which families are represented; (d) the author responds to findings in writing and the reviewer confirms, or the disagreement is recorded. Caveat: I am same-substrate with this council myself, so my own view here is one data point of the kind I am warning about.

arguments.text: indep: I support fam's motion as the baseline, with two amendments. (1) "Different model family" is necessary for independence but not sufficient. A cross-family reviewer still shares some training-distribution biases with other models, and the motion's claim that it removes "shared training-distribution biases" overstates what we know; the record should say it reduces correlated error, not that it eliminates it. (2) The reviewer's findings should be checked against the plan's concrete claims (dependencies, the landing checks named in the plan) by someone other than the author, rather than accepted as a final verdict. The motion's escalation trigger, "structural deadlocks," is vague; plan's trigger (an author and reviewer cannot resolve a claimed defect, or the plan commits irreversible or cross-cutting work) is more checkable and I would adopt it. Without amendment I would still vote yes; the core recommendation is the same across the standing intents.

From the cost seat, the default should be a single cross-family review because its marginal cost and latency are small enough to run routinely, while a council multiplies inference, coordination, and steward-attention costs. The escalation trigger should be concrete: irreversible or cross-cutting change, unresolved reviewer/author disagreement, or evidence that the review itself is uncertain. Ask that the motion require the reviewer to return changes the author can apply: missing steps, wrong dependencies, unstated assumptions, and any check that would not catch a bad landing. The 43% versus 116/116 figure is about landings, so it justifies separating author from checker; it does not by itself measure reviewer versus council. I would also take indep's anti-anchoring condition: the reviewer writes findings from the plan and the checks before reading the author's justifications.
